Dundubhi and the Test of the Seven Sal Trees

Stories from the Ramayana

Dundubhi and the Test of the Seven Sal Trees

Sugriva's Doubt, and Rama's Two Tests

In everyday English — Kishkindha Kanda, sargas 11–12

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read aloud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home and telling it to them.

The yellow boxes are the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little as you speak — Rama calm, Lakshmana quick, Sugriva worried, Dundubhi heavy and frightening, Vali proud.

(The purple cues) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

At the end of every part is a green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask the question. Let the listeners speak.

One part of this book carries a ◆ mark — the fight at the gate of Kishkindha. That part is not for younger listeners. The mark is written there before the part begins — you may skip that part, or tell it only to older listeners.

The main story of this book is from the Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, sargas 11–12. It is a story Sugriva himself tells Rama — a story inside a story. Anything more you may want to know is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — the young prince of Ayodhya. Tall, calm, kind. Warm dark-brown skin, black hair tied back, simple gold jewellery, a bow in his hand. In the forest he walks barefoot, his upper cloth worn.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother. Like Rama, but a little shorter and lighter in colour. Bow in hand, simple green-beige forest dress, barefoot.

Sugriva — king of the vanaras, son of the Sun. Warm brown fur, royal bearing, but now hiding from his elder brother Vali on Mount Rishyamuka.

Hanuman — the powerful vanara, light golden-brown fur, long tail, gentle devoted face, saffron dhoti. Sugriva's most trusted minister.

Vali — king of Kishkindha, son of Indra, Sugriva's elder brother. Immensely strong — he used to break the peaks of mountains.

Dundubhi — the great demon in the form of a buffalo. As large as Mount Kailasa, with the strength of a thousand elephants, drunk with pride in his boon.

Matanga — the great sage whose hermitage stands near Rishyamuka, on which drops of Dundubhi's blood fell.

The Ocean and Himavan — the Ocean, lord of rivers and storehouse of jewels; Himavan, king of mountains and father-in-law of Shankara, shelter of sages.

1 · Sugriva's Doubt · · SUGRIVA'S DOUBT

On Mount Rishyamuka, Rama and Sugriva had become friends — with fire as their witness, each had promised to help the other. Rama would win back Sugriva's kingdom from Vali, and Sugriva would help Rama in the search for Sita.

But in Sugriva's heart there was a doubt — a fear he could not hide.

One day he came to Rama and said, “Rama, you do not know Vali. Let me tell you what he is like.”

Sugriva said: “Vali would climb great mountains, break off their peaks and toss them into the sky — and then catch them again. The strongest trees of the forest he felled with his own strength. Such is his might.”

Rama listened in silence. Sugriva went on — “And there is a tale — the tale of Dundubhi. Hear it, and you will understand how strong Vali is.”

Lakshmana heard this and smiled.

Lakshmana said: “Sugriva, tell us — what would it take for you to believe that Rama can kill Vali?”

Sugriva thought and said, “Look, there lies the heap of Dundubhi's bones, and there stand the seven sal trees. If Rama can flick that heap two hundred bow-lengths with his foot, and pierce one sal tree with a single arrow — then I shall know that Vali is as good as dead at Rama's hands.”

Rama heard Sugriva's words — and smiled. “First tell me the tale of Dundubhi,” he said.

Pause and think — Sugriva had befriended Rama — yet doubt remained in his heart. Is it wrong to doubt inside a friendship? And what did Lakshmana do — he did not scold Sugriva, he asked: what proof would you need? Is that the right way to meet a doubt — not to demand trust, but to ask what proof would satisfy it?

2 · Dundubhi's Pride · · DUNDUBHI'S PRIDE

Sugriva began the tale — “Long ago there was a demon — Dundubhi. In the form of a buffalo he was as large as the peak of Mount Kailasa, and he carried the strength of a thousand elephants.”

Dundubhi had received a boon — and he was drunk with pride in that boon. He believed no one in the world was stronger than he. One day, as if Death itself were pushing him, he set out to find a great rival to fight.

First he went to the Ocean — lord of rivers, storehouse of jewels, king of waters.

Dundubhi roared: “Ocean! Come out — fight me!”

The Ocean was afraid. He knew how strong Dundubhi was. He said softly, “Dundubhi, I cannot fight you. But there is one who can give you the fight you want — Himavan, king of mountains. He is Shankara's father-in-law, shelter of sages, full of great waterfalls and caves. Go, fight him.”

Dundubhi reached Himavan with the speed of an arrow. There he smashed boulders as large as elephants and threw them down, and roared loudly.

Himavan said: “O skilled warrior Dundubhi, I am a mountain — I cannot fight you. But listen — in brilliant Kishkindha there lives a vanara — Vali. He is learned, glorious, and mighty like Indra. He alone is a rival worthy of you.”

When Dundubhi heard this, his eyes gleamed. Now he had found his rival — Vali.

Pause and think — Dundubhi went looking for a fight — first the Ocean, then Himavan, then Vali. The Ocean and Himavan refused to fight — were they cowards? Or did they know that a fight is not right everywhere? And Dundubhi — drunk with pride in his boon, why did he want to fight? Was the pride of strength itself leading him towards his death?

3 · The Fight at Kishkindha's Gate · · THE FIGHT AT KISHKINDHA'S GATE

◆ This part is not for younger listeners — this part tells of a fight between a demon and Vali.

Dundubhi took the form of a buffalo and arrived at the gate of Kishkindha. His horns were sharp, and he looked as terrible as a great dark rain-cloud — a cloud about to burst.

He let out a roar like the beating of a war-drum — the earth trembled. (Begin softly here, then roar loudly — as if a war-drum is sounding.)

Then he uprooted the trees nearby and threw them away, scraped the earth with his hooves, and like a maddened elephant he gored the city gate with his horns.

Vali heard the roar. He came out — he took off the garland given by his father Indra and set it aside, and leapt into the arena.

Vali seized Dundubhi by the horns — and a terrible fight began. With knees, with limbs, with boulders and trees — each fell upon the other.

Slowly Dundubhi's strength, his courage and his power began to fade — and Vali's strength grew with every moment. At last Vali lifted the huge Dundubhi — and dashed him to the earth.

With that fall Dundubhi's body broke — and his life left him. He fell to the ground — and never rose again.

Pause and think — Vali defeated Dundubhi — but was this fight necessary? Dundubhi had come asking for a fight — he had challenged the Ocean and Himavan too. When someone comes asking for a fight, what should be done? And Vali first took off Indra's garland and set it aside — why? Was he showing that he would fight with his own strength, not with the help of any boon?

4 · Matanga's Curse · · MATANGA'S CURSE

Dundubhi was dead — but the tale does not end there.

Vali, drunk with pride in his strength, lifted Dundubhi's dead body with both hands — and in a single flick hurled it a yojana away.

But as the body flew through the air, drops of blood from its mouth scattered and were carried by the wind — and they fell into the hermitage of the sage Matanga.

When the sage Matanga saw this, he was angry. His holy hermitage had been defiled. He spoke a curse —

The sage Matanga said: “He who has defiled my hermitage — that Vali shall never be able to come into this Rishyamuka region. If he comes here, his head will shatter into pieces.”

From that day Vali never came near Rishyamuka — he could not come. And that is why Sugriva lived safely in this forest with his ministers.

Sugriva showed Rama — “Look, Rama — that heap of bones, shining like a mountaintop — that is Dundubhi, whom Vali hurled away in the pride of his strength.”

“And look there — the seven great sal trees, their branches spread wide. Vali would shake one tree — and in a single shake all its leaves would fall. Such is his strength. So tell me, Rama — who can defeat him in battle?”

Pause and think — Vali defeated Dundubhi — but by flinging the dead body he defiled the sage's hermitage. After a victory, is care still needed? And Matanga's curse — a punishment for Vali — became protection for Sugriva. Can someone's punishment ever become someone else's protection?

5 · The First Test — the Skeleton · · THE FIRST TEST — THE SKELETON

Sugriva named his conditions — “Rama, if you can flick this withered body of Dundubhi two hundred bow-lengths with your foot, and pierce one sal tree with a single arrow — then I shall know that Vali is as good as dead at your hands.”

Rama heard Sugriva's words — and stepped forward, smiling.

He did not even lift his foot — he only, sportively, flicked the withered body of the demon with his big toe. (Pause here — and say it slowly, as if a wonder is happening.)

And that body — that great heap of bones — flew through the air and fell ten yojanas away!

Sugriva stood watching in amazement. Rama had done far more than the condition asked — two hundred bow-lengths was asked, and Rama had thrown it ten yojanas!

But one test still remained in Sugriva's mind — the test of the sal trees.

Pause and think — Rama flicked the heap of bones with his big toe — without lifting his foot, as if in play. Does this show how effortless Rama's strength was — as if even a great task were play to him? And Sugriva had asked for two hundred bow-lengths — Rama did ten yojanas. How does it feel when someone does far more than was expected?

6 · The Second Test — the Seven Sal Trees · · THE SECOND TEST — THE SEVEN SAL TREES

Now came the turn of the sal trees. Seven great sal trees stood in a row — their branches spread wide, full of leaves.

Rama took up his dreadful bow — and fitted a single golden arrow.

As he drew the bowstring, its twang filled all the directions. (Let your voice echo here — as if the twang of the bow can be heard.)

And then — a single arrow flew.

That golden arrow pierced all seven sal trees as it passed — it pierced even the heights of the mountain — and went down into the earth.

And then, in a single moment — that arrow came up again from beneath the earth — and swiftly returned into Rama's quiver!

Sugriva saw the seven pierced sal trees — and fell into the greatest wonder.

Sugriva said: “O Kakutstha! He who has ripped off seven great sal trees, a mountain and the earth with a single arrow — who can stand before him in the vanguard of war? With your arrows you could defeat all the gods, Indra included — then what of Vali!”

Rama smiled and said, “Then, Sugriva, wear a garland and challenge Vali once more. By the garland I shall know you apart — and I shall not strike you, but him.”

Sugriva's doubt was gone. Now he knew — Rama could defeat Vali.

Pause and think — One arrow — seven trees, a mountain, the earth — and then the arrow returned to the quiver. Is this only a tale of strength? Or does it also say that true strength is shown not for display, but to remove a friend's doubt? And why did Rama speak of the garland — because in battle the two brothers look alike, and Rama never wanted to strike his own friend?

Bigger Thoughts · · BIGGER THOUGHTS

In this tale there are three stories — a demon who died in pride; a king who won and yet received a curse; and a friend whose doubt was removed by two tests.

Dundubhi was strong — but his strength led him to seek out a fight, and that became his death. Vali was strong — but in the pride of victory he flung a dead body, and received a curse. And Rama was strong — but he showed his strength to remove a friend's doubt.

Ask the listeners:

1. Dundubhi received a boon — but he became drunk with pride in it. Is pride in a boon or in strength dangerous?

2. The Ocean and Himavan refused to fight Dundubhi. Is refusing to fight cowardice — or wisdom?

3. Vali defeated Dundubhi — but by flinging the dead body he defiled the sage's hermitage. Why is care needed even after a victory?

4. Matanga's curse was a punishment for Vali — but it became protection for Sugriva. Can someone's punishment become someone else's protection?

5. Sugriva had befriended Rama — yet doubt remained in his heart. Is it wrong to have doubt inside a friendship?

6. Rama flicked the heap of bones with his big toe — as if in play. Is true strength effortless — without display?

7. Why did Rama speak of the garland — that Sugriva should wear it when he goes? Because in battle, knowing your own friend apart is the most important thing?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source

The main story of this book is from the Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, sargas 11–12 — Sugriva's doubt, the tale of Dundubhi, Matanga's curse, and Rama's two tests.

Sugriva's Doubt — Sarga 11

Sugriva's account of Vali's strength — breaking the peaks of mountains, tossing them into the sky and catching them, felling sturdy trees — and Lakshmana smiling and asking what proof would convince him, is at the beginning of sarga 11.

Dundubhi's Pride — Sarga 11

Dundubhi's buffalo form, his Kailasa-like size, the strength of a thousand elephants, his pride in his boon, his challenge to the Ocean, the Ocean's fearful direction to Himavan, and Himavan's direction to Vali — this is in sarga 11.

The Fight at Kishkindha's Gate — Sarga 11

Dundubhi's arrival at the gate of Kishkindha — his roar like a war-drum, uprooting trees, scraping the earth with his hooves, goring the gate with his horns — Vali setting aside Indra's garland and coming out, seizing him by the horns, fighting with knees, limbs, boulders and trees, and lifting Dundubhi and dashing him to the earth — this is in sarga 11.

Matanga's Curse — Sarga 11

Vali hurling Dundubhi's dead body a yojana away, drops of blood falling with the wind into Matanga's hermitage, Matanga's curse — Vali barred from the Rishyamuka region, his head to shatter into pieces if he entered — and Sugriva therefore living safely there — this is in sarga 11.

The Heap of Bones and the Seven Sal Trees — Sarga 11

The heap of bones shining like a mountaintop, the seven great sal trees with their spreading branches, Vali shaking one tree and making all its leaves fall at once, and Sugriva's conditions — flicking the heap two hundred bow-lengths with the foot, piercing one tree with one arrow — this is in sarga 11.

The First Test — Sarga 11

Rama sportively flicking Dundubhi's withered body ten yojanas with his big toe — without lifting his foot — is at the end of sarga 11.

The Second Test — Sarga 12

Rama taking up his bow, piercing all seven sal trees, the mountain heights and the earth with one golden arrow, the arrow coming up in a moment from beneath the earth and returning to the quiver, Sugriva's great wonder, and Rama asking Sugriva to wear a garland and challenge Vali again — this is in sarga 12.

The Meaning of the Name Dundubhi

‘Dundubhi’ means a war-drum. The demon's roar was like a war-drum, and so he was named Dundubhi.

What Happens Next

Sugriva will wear the garland and go to challenge Vali — and Rama, hidden, will strike Vali with an arrow. That tale is in the next books of this series.

The End · · THE END

Here the tale of Dundubhi and the test of the seven sal trees comes to rest — a demon's pride, a king's curse, and a friend's doubt, removed by two tests.

And whenever a task seems too great, remember Rama's big toe, which flicked a heap of bones ten yojanas away as if in play. And whenever you doubt someone, remember Lakshmana — who did not scold, but asked: what proof would you need?

— The End —
